question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Applying Several Elementary Operations
question.problem: Suppose $U$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(U)=21.$ The matrix $V$ is obtained from $U$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{4}$ and ${R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(V)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{4}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{1}{3},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{1}{3}$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $\frac{1}{3}.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(V) & =\frac{1}{3}det(U) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 21 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying a Row Operation Given the Connection Between Two Determinants
question.problem:
Consider the matrices given below. Given that $X$ and $Y$ are row equivalent matrices and $det(X)=-60$, find $det(Y).$

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,Y=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that $Y$ can be obtained from $X$ by swapping the $1$st and the $3$rd rows. 

This changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.
Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =-det(X) \\  & =-(-60) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Identifying a Row Operation Given the Connection Between Two Determinants
question.problem:
Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3}.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Visualizing Intersections of Uncountable Families of Indexed Sets
question.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,i]\times [0,1].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,0.5]\times [0,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,0.5],b\in [0,1]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(0.5,0),$ $(0.5,1),$ and $(0,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/5b882f3fb0e7b44eb2df3a510260574e5c4a4d85842a9c0d65515f1a40894756.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,i]\times [0,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,i],b\in [0,1]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(i,0),$ $(i,1),$ and $(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/cb530698591dbd71a8058d9faa0c60b636dc654f21e92d65ec8295aeaa67355a.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $\{0\}\times [0,1]:$

question.knowledge_point: Sketching Cartesian Products of Special Sets in the Coordinate Plane
question.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=R\times N$ in the Cartesian plane?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times N
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in N\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/f8808e4c35775c754dab0bf328a8d129e423009e18ec5f4b962461eba2afcea2.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $2.$

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(x,2)\,:\,x\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082768/assets/a51fe9dc5bf7c55b01f72a45d4b88bde4653f0d3da85c1231b0d54c76a6e8c81.png)

We can create the subsets ${S}_{3},{S}_{4},{S}_{5},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & ={S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup {S}_{3}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times N$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

question.knowledge_point: Solving for One Coefficient in a Linear Combination
question.worked_solution:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $h$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{a}_{1}+h{a}_{2} & =b \\ 3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+h[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ h[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 14 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ h[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

From the final equation above, we can tell that $h=2.$

$$

$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving for Two Coefficients in a Linear Combination
question.problem:
Consider the vectors

$$
{c}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,d=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}=d,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$
.
question.worked_solution:
If ${x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}=d,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -11 \\ -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3 \\ 4{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-11 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the second and the third  equations we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}_{1} & =-16\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${x}_{1}=-2$ into the third equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-2)+{x}_{2}=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=3$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & =3 \\ (-2)+2(3) & =3 \\ 4 & =3,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a false statement. 

So, the system has no solution.

question.knowledge_point: Solving for Two Coefficients in a Linear Combination
question.problem:
Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-7 \\ -{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-1 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=6\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the first and the second equation we get

$$
-2{x}_{2}=-8\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=4.
$$

Substituting ${x}_{2}=4$ into the first equation yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} & =-7 \\ {x}_{1}-(4) & =-7 \\ {x}_{1} & =-7+4 \\ {x}_{1} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=-3$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ into the third equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} & =6 \\ 2(-3)+3(4) & =6 \\ 6 & =6,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=-3$ and ${x}_{2}=4,$ which means

$$
-3{a}_{1}+4{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-3+4=1.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving for Three Coefficients in a Linear Combination
question.problem:
Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -8 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$
question.worked_solution:
If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -8 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ -8{x}_{2} \\ 6{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=2\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=-5 \\ {x}_{3}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=6.$ Substituting ${x}_{3}=6$ into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{2}-6=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting ${x}_{2}=1$ and ${x}_{3}=6$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-3(1)+2(6)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-7.
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=-7$, ${x}_{2}=1$, and ${x}_{3}=6,$ which means 

$$
-7{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+6{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-7+1+6=0.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Solving for Three Coefficients in a Linear Combination
question.problem:
Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$
question.worked_solution:
If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ 0 \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -10 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=-5 \\ 5{x}_{3}=-10 \\ 3{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1\end{aligned}
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10 \\ 0 & 2 & -5 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & -5 & 16 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2.5 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2.5 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=-5 \\ {x}_{2}-2.5\,{x}_{3}=8 \\ {x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=-2.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get 

$$
{x}_{2}-2.5(-2)=8\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=8-5=3.
$$

Finally,  substituting ${x}_{2}=3$ and ${x}_{3}=-2$  into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-(3)+2(-2)=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=2$, ${x}_{2}=3$, and ${x}_{3}=-2,$ which means 

$$
2{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}-2{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=2+3-2=3.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors
question.problem:
The vectors ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ from the decomposition $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ {x}_{2}=1 \\ 2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=7\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ {x}_{2}=1 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=1.$ Substituting into the first equation gives 

$$
{x}_{1}-1=1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Since the system has a solution, we can conclude that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}.$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & =b \\ 2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 1=2.$
